case_study_insert.main_stem: Ridgeway Quality Castings (RQC) is a private limited company in the foundry sector, making iron castings for agricultural machinery and serving four regional equipment makers, with a workforce of 110. Founded in 2003 by Tomas Ridgeway, it operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. RQC plans to invest $960,000 in a sand-casting moulding line using recycled metal feedstock, financed by a $560,000 bank loan and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $16.00 a unit and a selling price of $28.00, and produces 50,000 units a year. RQC reports waste of 6.8% and labour turnover of 12%, raising unit costs across the foundry.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Foundry Operations Report — Q1 2025: 12,400 castings were poured; the scrap rate was 6.8%, down from 9.3%. There were 54 quality complaints from agricultural-machinery customers. Energy use is 3.4 kWh per casting, and 78% of melt is recycled. Average order lead time is 23 days. A survey of 410 buyers found 66% prefer castings with recycled content and 58% would pay $0.80 more for certified low-waste production.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Ridgeway Quality Castings as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base interest rate increased from 4.00% to 4.75%, raising borrowing costs for leveraged firms. (2) The minimum wage went up 6.2% to $13.90 per hour. (3) Scrap-metal and energy input costs rose 10.5% year-on-year, while foundry equipment inflation was 7.4% and agricultural machinery demand fell 1.6%.

questions.question_text: RQC plans to fund its sand-casting line with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for RQC of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using $400,000 retained profit avoids interest on that part of the $960,000 scheme, easing cash flow while RQC already carries fixed costs of $480,000 a year and a $560,000 loan. The saving can be spent on reducing the 6.8% waste rate and the $13.90 wage pressure, protecting the $12.00 contribution on 50,000 castings.

Point 2: Retained profit needs no security and leaves control with Tomas Ridgeway, so the hierarchical structure can act quickly on the 12% labour turnover problem without lender conditions. It also avoids piling more debt onto a foundry already exposed to the 4.75% base rate.

For a foundry with 110 workers and $480,000 fixed costs, retained profit also avoids the 4.75% rate environment on $400,000 of the scheme. The $560,000 loan must still be served, but keeping the $400,000 internal protects the $12.00 contribution on 50,000 castings and the 10,000-unit margin of safety while 12% turnover is tackled.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: RQC is launching certified low-waste castings. Consider agricultural trade magazines, a machinery exhibition, or direct mail to its four equipment makers. Which should RQC choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Agricultural trade magazines: They reach equipment makers cheaply and can explain the 78% recycled melt rate to engineers, but a printed message cannot prove the fall in scrap from 9.3% to 6.8% and competes with many rivals.

Machinery exhibition: A stand allows live display of castings and discussion of the $0.80 premium that 58% of surveyed buyers accept. It builds trust for the $960,000 recycled-feedstock line, but stand costs are high and four regional customers dominate sales, so most visitors would not be buyers.

Direct mail to the four equipment makers: Tailored technical packs can show inspection records, the 54-complaint reduction target and the 23-day lead time directly to the people who decide. It is inexpensive and measurable, though reach is limited to existing accounts.

The four equipment makers drive most demand, so a $960,000 investment is justified only by keeping their orders; with $12.00 contribution, even a small retention gain matters more than unqualified exhibition leads. Direct mail can show the 23-day lead time and the fall in scrap from 9.3% to 6.8%, the evidence behind the 58% premium, which a magazine cannot verify. An exhibition would also expose quality before the moulding line is stable.

Recommendation: RQC should choose direct mail to its four equipment makers, backed by a small magazine campaign. It targets the actual buyers and supports the 66% preference for recycled content. The exhibition is rejected as expensive and broad; magazines alone are rejected because they cannot demonstrate the certified quality that justifies the $0.80 premium.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two promotional options applied to RQC with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discussion of all three options in context with a justified recommendation rejecting the exhibition and magazines alone.

questions.question_text: RQC has labour turnover of 12% and hierarchical leadership. Explain two benefits for RQC of using financial motivators such as a bonus for its workforce of 110.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A bonus linked to the scrap rate gives the 110 foundry workers a direct financial reason to cut the 6.8% waste figure, which would lower the $16.00 variable cost per unit and protect the $12.00 contribution. Under Herzberg, pay is a hygiene factor that removes dissatisfaction, so it can stabilise the 12% turnover.

Point 2: A gain-sharing bonus tied to the 54 customer complaints would encourage teams to improve quality on the $960,000 moulding line. Tomas Ridgeway can use the democratic style within the hierarchy to agree fair targets, raising commitment and reducing the rework that pushes unit cost above the $25.60 benchmark while 50,000 units are produced.

Productivity of 50,000 units divided by 110 workers is 454.55 units per worker, showing why stability matters: losing experienced staff to 12% turnover raises rework and the 6.8% scrap rate. A bonus tied to the 54 complaints and the 78% recycled melt gives measurable goals under democratic leadership within the hierarchy.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: RQC wants to cut its 6.8% waste rate. Consider quality circles or final inspection (quality control). Which should RQC choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Quality circles: Regular worker groups can identify the causes of 6.8% scrap, using the experience of the 110 staff and the 78% recycled-melt data. Prevention lowers the $16.00 cost at source and suits democratic leadership, but it takes time and needs commitment, which is harder while labour turnover is 12%.

Final inspection: Checking castings before dispatch would quickly reduce the 54 complaints and protect the $28.00 price, giving visible results. However, it finds waste only after energy of 3.4 kWh per casting has been used, so the 6.8% scrap bill remains and the $960,000 line's efficiency is not improved.

Measurement should use the 6.8% scrap rate, the 54 complaints and the 3.4 kWh per casting, with monthly review while the $960,000 line is commissioned. The insert states no meeting costs or training fees, so none are invented; the decision rests on preventing waste at source across 50,000 units and protecting the 10,000-unit margin of safety. With 12% labour turnover, circles must include new starters or knowledge of the 78% recycled-melt process will be lost, whereas inspection alone would leave the $16.00 unit cost unchanged. Quality circles fit the democratic style within RQC's hierarchy and give the 110 workers ownership of the change, which makes prevention sustainable.

The 10,000-unit margin of safety depends on it.

Decision: RQC should choose quality circles, with inspection retained as a safety net. They attack the cause of waste and protect contribution; pure inspection is rejected because it detects defects after the cost is incurred and cannot deliver the 58%-premium quality consistently.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies relevant factors with limited application to the named business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of quality circles and inspection applied to RQC's waste problem.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluation of both approaches in context with a justified decision rejecting inspection-led control.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how RQC's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $480,000 ÷ ($28.00 − $16.00) = $480,000 ÷ $12.00 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $28.00 − $16.00 = $12.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways RQC's management can use this cost, break-even and productivity data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the break-even output of 40,000 units with actual production of 50,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 10,000 units, so they know how far demand can fall before RQC makes a loss.
2. Contribution per unit of $12.00 shows what each unit adds towards fixed costs of $480,000; for illustration, a $1.00 price cut would reduce contribution to $11.00 and raise break-even to 43,636.36 units, letting managers test pricing before committing.
3. Average total cost of $25.60 a unit ($480,000 ÷ 50,000 units plus $16.00 variable cost) provides a benchmark each quarter to track the 6.8% waste and 12% labour turnover and decide whether rework is pushing unit cost above plan.
4. Labour productivity of 454.55 units per worker (50,000 units ÷ workforce of 110) shows whether the $960,000 investment can be handled by the existing team, or whether recruitment is needed before the wage bill rises.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $12.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 50,000 units; illustrative pricing and the $480,000 fixed costs; the $960,000 investment decision; and unit-cost and productivity benchmarking to tackle the 6.8% waste and 12% labour turnover.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate RQC's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has RQC's financial position improved? Which of the two ratios is the stronger evidence? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.56 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.79 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.78 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.05 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $175,000 inventories + $130,000 trade receivables + $45,000 cash = $350,000; 2025 current assets = $160,000 + $155,000 + $70,000 = $385,000. For 2024, $350,000 ÷ $225,000 = 1.56, and ($350,000 − $175,000) ÷ $225,000 = 0.78. For 2025, $385,000 ÷ $215,000 = 1.79, and ($385,000 − $160,000) ÷ $215,000 = 1.05. All source figures are the $'000 values in Appendix 2.

Evaluation: Liquidity has strengthened on both measures, so RQC's short-term financial position has improved. Cash rose from $45,000 to $70,000 and current liabilities fell from $225,000 to $215,000, strengthening liquidity for the $560,000 loan, but receivables grew from $130,000 to $155,000, so working capital is increasingly tied up with the four equipment makers.
The acid test ratio is the stronger evidence of real improvement because it rose from 0.78 to 1.05 without relying on inventories, which are the least liquid current asset.

No sector benchmark is given, and a 1.79 current ratio could reflect slow-moving inventory rather than strength. The $155,000 receivables from four buyers are a concentration risk; if one pays late, the 2025 improvement could reverse.

Conclusion: RQC's financial position has improved: both liquidity measures are higher in 2025 and the gain survives the exclusion of inventories. Tomas Ridgeway should tighten credit control before the $960,000 moulding line is fully paid for.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies relevant factors with limited application to the named business.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for both years with some contextual comment on the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities, an explicit answer on the stronger ratio, and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for RQC of using recycled metal feedstock in its new sand-casting line.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled feedstock supports the 66% of surveyed buyers who prefer recycled content and the 58% who would pay $0.80 more, protecting the $12.00 contribution on 50,000 castings. It also reduces exposure to the 10.5% rise in scrap-metal and energy costs and helps lower the 6.8% waste figure.

Disadvantage: Recycled metal can vary in quality, which could raise the 54 complaints and the 6.8% scrap rate unless sorting is tight. The insert does not decompose the $16.00 variable cost, so RQC cannot quantify the saving, and the $960,000 line adds fixed costs that must be covered by 40,000 units of break-even output.

Recycled feedstock should be judged against the 40,000-unit break-even and $480,000 fixed costs: if melt quality varies, the 6.8% scrap rate could rise and absorption of the $960,000 line would slip. The insert gives no price for recycled metal, so no saving is quantified; the 66% buyer preference is the defensible benefit.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase to $13.90 and the 10.5% rise in scrap-metal and energy input costs will affect RQC. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
RQC faces three external changes reported in Appendix 3.

Base interest rate 4.00% to 4.75%: If the $560,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.0075 × $560,000 bank loan = $4,200 a year (0.0075 × 560,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $480,000 and the $960,000 investment, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it completely, though future borrowing would cost more and customers may cut spending.

Minimum wage up 6.2% to $13.90: With a workforce of 110, this raises the wage bill on every production hour and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay rates, so no defensible annual total can be invented; against the given productivity of 454.55 units per worker, the rise is absorbable only if output per worker holds, otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $12.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

10.5% scrap-metal and energy input costs: The insert does not decompose the $16.00 variable cost per unit, so only a labelled upper-bound illustration is honest: if the entire $16.00 were exposed, the rise would add 0.105 × $16.00 = $1.68 a unit, or $84,000 a year at 50,000 units. The bound is far larger than the $4,200 interest rise, so feedstock prices are the dominant financial threat.

Conclusion: the 10.5% rise in scrap-metal and energy input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 50,000 units, directly erodes the $12.00 contribution that justifies the $960,000 plan, and dwarfs the $4,200 interest effect; the wage rise is material but cannot be quantified from the insert. Tomas Ridgeway should secure recycled-metal supply contracts and promote the $0.80 low-waste premium.
